A population, $P$, which is initially 5000, varies according to the formula

$$P=5000b^{\frac{-t}{10}},$$

where $b$ is a positive constant and $t$ is time in years, $t\ge 0$.

The population is 1250 after 20 years.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of decrease is 30 people per year.

solutions.latex:
$$P = 5000b^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
When $t = 20$, $P = 1250$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1250 &= 5000\,b^{-2} \\ b^{-2} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ b &= 2 \quad (b > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 5000(2)^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 5000\times\ln 2\times\dfrac{-1}{10}\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}}$$
Find $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -30$:
$$\begin{aligned} -30 &= -500\times\ln 2\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{500\ln 2}{30} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= 11.55\ldots \\ \dfrac{t}{10}\ln 2 &= \ln 11.55\ldots \\ t &= 35.3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Equates $-30$ to a correct derivative, with $b = 2$, or equivalent merit
Finds $b$ and provides correct derivative, or equivalent merit
Provides correct derivative, or equivalent merit

$$P(t)=400\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right),\ 0\le t\le 12,$$

Show that $E=\dfrac{4800}{\pi}\left(\cos\dfrac{a\pi}{12}-\cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12}\right)$.

157.stem:
A scientist is studying the growth of bacteria. The scientist models the number of bacteria, $N$, by the equation

$$N(t)=200e^{0.013t},$$

where $t$ is the number of hours after starting the experiment.

parts.latex: What is the initial number of bacteria in the experiment?
What is the number of bacteria 24 hours after starting the experiment?
What is the rate of increase in the number of bacteria 24 hours after starting the experiment?

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} N(0) &= 200e^{0} \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} N(24) &= 200e^{0.013 \times 24} \\ &= 273.23\ldots \\ &\approx 273 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 200 \times 0.013 \times e^{0.013t}$$
When $t = 24$,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt} &= 0.013 \times 273 \quad \text{(from part (b))} \\ &= 3.55 \end{aligned}$$
Rate of increase $= 3.55$ bacteria/hour.

254.stem:
Recycled plastic materials can contain bacteria from previous usage. To ensure the plastic is clean and safe for recycling, it is heated to $135^\circ\text{C}$ for a certain period to kill the bacteria present.

The number of bacteria $N$ in the plastic after $t$ minutes at $135^\circ\text{C}$ is given by:
$$N(t)=4800e^{-0.3t}, \quad t\ge 0$$

parts.latex: Find the initial number of bacteria present in the plastic.
Find the time in minutes to kill 50% of the bacteria. Give your answer correct to the nearest second.
Find the rate of decrease of the bacteria after 5 minutes. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
$$N(t) = 50\%\times 4800 = 2400$$
$$\begin{aligned} 4800e^{-0.3t} &= 2400 \\ e^{-0.3t} &= 0.5 \\ -0.3t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ t &= -\dfrac{\ln(0.5)}{0.3} \\ &= 2.310\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ t \approx 2$ minutes $19$ seconds.

257.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line with acceleration $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=1-2t$, for $0\le t\le 2$.

The particle was initially at rest at the origin.

parts.latex: Determine $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ as a function of $t$.
Sketch the graph of $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ for $0\le t\le 2$ below, showing any stationary points, end points and intercepts with the axes.
Find the distance travelled over the first two seconds.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= \int (1 - 2t)\,dt \\ &= t - t^2 + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = C = 0$.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dx}{dt} = t - t^2$$
\exfigure{408_q25_s1}

$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= \int_0^1 \left(t - t^2\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \int_1^2 \left(t - t^2\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_1^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{4}{2} - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \text{Total distance} &= \dfrac{1}{6} + \left|-\dfrac{5}{6}\right| \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line such that its acceleration with respect to time is given by $a=-2t+3$, where $a$ is the acceleration of the particle at time $t$ seconds for $t\ge 0$.

The particle is at rest when $t=1$ and $t=2$.

Which of the following graphs best represents the displacement of the particle?

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$v = \int(-2t+3)\,dt = -t^2 + 3t + C$$
The particle is at rest at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, so $v = 0$ there:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 + 3 + C &= 0 \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$v = -t^2 + 3t - 2 = -(t-1)(t-2)$$
Sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &< 0 &&\text{for } 0 \le t < 1 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\\ v &> 0 &&\text{for } 1 < t < 2 &&\text{displacement increasing}\\ v &< 0 &&\text{for } t > 2 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the displacement has a local minimum at $t = 1$ and a local maximum at $t = 2$.

Graph A is the only graph with a minimum at $t = 1$, a maximum at $t = 2$ and decreasing afterwards. (Graph B has the turning points the wrong way round; C and D do not have stationary points at both $t = 1$ and $t = 2$.)

The rate of fuel consumption of a particular vehicle may be modelled by the formula

$$R=5+4e^{-0.5t},$$

where $R$ is the rate of fuel consumption, in litres per hour, after $t$ hours of travel.

In the first hour of travel, the vehicle consumed 25 litres of fuel.

Determine the amount of fuel consumed after 4 hours of travel, correct to the nearest litre.

solutions.latex:
The amount of fuel, $F(t)$ litres, consumed at time $t$ hours is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int R\,dt \\ &= \int 5+4e^{-0.5t}\,dt \\ &= 5t-8e^{-0.5t}+c \end{aligned}$$

At time $t=1$, the vehicle has consumed 25 litres of fuel since the start of the journey.

Finding the constant of integration, $c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 25 &= 5(1)-8e^{-0.5(1)}+c \\ 20 &= -8e^{-0.5}+c \\ c &= 20+8e^{-0.5} \end{aligned}$$

At time $t=4$, the amount of fuel the vehicle consumed is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F &= 5(4)-8e^{-0.5(4)}+20+8e^{-0.5} \\ &= 43.7695\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ After 4 hours of travel, the vehicle has consumed 44 litres of fuel.
criteria: Finds the value of the constant of integration, or equivalent merit

314.stem:
The velocity of a particle is given by $v=2\sin\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ metres per second.

Find:

figures.cap: blank v vs t axes for answer

parts.latex: the equation of the displacement $x$ of the particle as a function of time if the particle is initially at the origin.
when the particle comes to rest for first time.
the exact initial velocity.
the maximum speed of the particle.
Using your graph above or otherwise, find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first $\pi$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
$$x = \int 2\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)dt = -2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -2\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C \\ 0 &= -2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 1 - 2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
At rest means $v = 0$: $\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$, so $t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 0, \pi, \dots$

$\therefore$ The first time with $t \ge 0$ is $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} v(0) &= 2\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 2\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= -\sqrt{3} \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

$v=2\sin\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$. Start from the range of sine:
$$\begin{aligned} -1&\le \sin\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\le 1\\ -2&\le v\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ The maximum speed is $|v|_{\max} = 2$ m/s. (It occurs, for example, at $t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.)

$v = 2\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is the graph of $y = 2\sin t$ shifted $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the right. It has amplitude $2$ and period $2\pi$.

\exfigure{568_q15_s1}
criteria: Shows the intercepts $(0,-\sqrt{3})$, $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit
Draws the correct shape (shifted sine, amplitude $2$) over $[0,2\pi]$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so split the time interval there. Using $x = 1 - 2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ from (i):
$$x(0) = 0, \qquad x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1 - 2\cos 0 = -1, \qquad x(\pi) = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = 1 + 1 = 2$$
Distance for $0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{3}$: $|-1 - 0| = 1$ m.

Distance for $\dfrac{\pi}{3} \le t \le \pi$: $|2 - (-1)| = 3$ m.

$\therefore$ Total distance $= 1 + 3 = 4$ m.

32.stem:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $a=2e^{-t}\text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Initially it is 2 metres to the right of $O$ and is moving towards $O$ with speed $1\text{ ms}^{-1}$.

parts.latex: Show that $v=1-2e^{-t}$ and $x=t+2e^{-t}$.
Find in simplest exact form when and where the particle is at rest.
Find in simplest exact form the distance travelled by the particle in the first $\ln 8$ seconds of its motion.

solutions.latex:
$a=2e^{-t}$

$v=-2e^{-t}+c$

When $t=0$, $v=-1$, so $-1=-2+c$.

$\therefore\ c=1$

$\therefore\ v=1-2e^{-t}$

$x=t+2e^{-t}+d$

When $t=0$, $x=2$, so $2=2+d$.

$\therefore\ d=0$

$\therefore\ x=t+2e^{-t}$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds $v$ in terms of $t$

meta.top_criterion_original: Uses integration to find required expressions for both $v$ and $x$ in terms of $t$

solutions.latex:
When $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^{-t}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ e^t&=2\\ \therefore\ t&=\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=t+2e^{-t}\\ &=\ln 2+2\times\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=1+\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
At rest $(1+\ln 2)$ m to the right of $O$ at time $\ln 2$ seconds.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds time when particle at rest

meta.top_criterion_original: Finds time and position when particle at rest

solutions.latex:
When $t=\ln 8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\ln 8+2e^{\ln\frac{1}{8}}\\ &=3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Hence in the first $\ln 8$ seconds:

the particle travels left $2-(1+\ln 2)$ metres,

then is instantaneously at rest before moving off to the right (since $a>0$),

travelling a further $\left(3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)-(1+\ln 2)$ metres.

Required distance is $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}+\ln 2\right)$ metres.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds simplified expression for $x$ when $t=\ln 8$

551.stem:
Radioactive cobalt-60 decays to become nickel-60. A 1000 g block of radioactive cobalt-60 is placed in a container.

After a period of 10.54 years, $75\%$ of the cobalt-60 has decayed to become nickel-60.

The decay process can be modelled by the exponential relationship

$$A=1000e^{kt}$$

where $A$ is the amount of cobalt-60 remaining (in grams) at time $t$ (in years).

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$, correct to 4 decimal places.
Find the value of $t$ when the rate of change of $A$ is $-9.48$ g/year, correct to the nearest year.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $A=1000e^{kt}$:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-9.48$ with $k=-0.1315$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(-0.1315)e^{-0.1315t}&=-9.48\\ e^{-0.1315t}&=\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\\ -0.1315t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\right)\\ t&\approx20.0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx20 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$ and equates it to $-9.48$, or equivalent merit

Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{f(t)}=f'(t)e^{f(t)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\ &=-\big(-\pi\sin(\pi t)\big)e^{\cos(\pi t)}\\ &=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}\end{aligned}$$

589.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis. Its velocity in metres per second, at time $t$ seconds, is given by

$$v=\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1.$$

parts.latex: Find the time at which the particle is stationary.
Find the acceleration of the particle when it is stationary.
The total distance travelled by the particle in the first two seconds is $\ln b$ metres, for some constant $b>0$. Find the value of $b$.

solutions.latex:
Stationary when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{t+1}-1&=0 \\ \dfrac{2}{t+1}&=1 \\ 2&=t+1 \\ t&=1\text{ second} \end{aligned}$$

Acceleration $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, with $v=2(t+1)^{-1}-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-2(t+1)^{-2} \\ &=-\dfrac{2}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$ (from part (a)):
$$a(1)=-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ ms}^{-2}$$

$a<0$ for all $t$ and $v=0$ at $t=1$, so
$$\begin{aligned} v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right} \\ v&<0 &&\text{for } 1<t\le 2 &&\text{moving left} \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the first second:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\left(\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1\right)dt&=\Big[2\ln|t+1|-t\Big]_0^1 \\ &=2\ln 2-1 \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the next second (velocity negative):
$$\begin{aligned} \Big[t-2\ln|t+1|\Big]_1^2&=2-2\ln 3-(1-2\ln 2) \\ &=1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Total distance:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\ln 2-1+1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2&=4\ln 2-2\ln 3 \\ &=\ln 2^4-\ln 3^2 \\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
criteria: Finds both distances, $2\ln 2-1$ for $0\le t\le 1$ and $1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2$ for $1\le t\le 2$, or equivalent merit

A population of insects varies according to the formula $P = 3000n^{\frac{t}{10}}$, where $n$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the time in days.

The initial population was 3000. After 20 days the population had grown to 12 000.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of increase is 6000 insects per day.

solutions.latex:
Initially $P=3000$; after 20 days $P=12\,000$. Find $n$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12000 &= 3000n^{\frac{20}{10}} \\ n^2 &= 4 \\ n &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}$$
$n > 0$, so $n = 2$ and $P=3000\times 2^{\frac{t}{10}}$.

Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 3000 \times \ln 2 \times \dfrac{1}{10} \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 6000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{20}{\ln 2} \\ \dfrac{t}{10} &= \log_2\left(\dfrac{20}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \log_2 20 - \log_2(\ln 2) \\ t &= 10\left(\dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 2} - \dfrac{\ln(\ln 2)}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &\approx 48.5 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Three of: finds $n$, finds $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, substitutes 6000 into $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, calculates $t$ (or 1 error), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} v(t)&=3\sqrt{t+1}-9\\ &=3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\\ x(t)&=\int\left(3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\right)dt\\ &=\dfrac{3(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C\\ &=2\sqrt{(t+1)^3}-9t+C\\ &=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t+C \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at $O$, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=2(1)\sqrt{1}-9(0)+C\\ \therefore\ C&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2 \text{ as required}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates $v(t)$ but does not evaluate the constant of integration or makes an error, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9&=0\\ \sqrt{t+1}&=3\\ t+1&=9\\ \therefore\ t&=8 \end{aligned}$$
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} x(8)&=2(8+1)\sqrt{8+1}-9(8)-2\\ &=-20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The particle is at rest after 8 seconds, 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of motion.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=20+20+32\\ &=72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

899.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis such that at a time $t$ seconds its displacement from the origin is $x$ metres. The acceleration of the particle is given by $a=\dfrac{8}{e^{2t}}+\dfrac{3}{e^t}$.

Initially its velocity is $-6$ m/s and its displacement is 5 m.

At what time and where does the particle come to rest?

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: v and x were found in part (a); this part solves v=0 and evaluates x, covered by agreed skills.

e and natural logarithms.reason: ln step is part of the agreed Exponential equations; x evaluated to decimals, e^{ln} property not needed.

solutions.latex:
$$a=8e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}$$
Integrating to find the velocity:
$$v=\dfrac{8e^{-2t}}{-2}+\dfrac{3e^{-t}}{-1}+c$$
When $t=0$, $v=-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} -6&=-4e^0-3e^0+c\\ -6&=-7+c\\ c&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$v=-4e^{-2t}-3e^{-t}+1$$
Integrating again:
$$x=\dfrac{-4e^{-2t}}{-2}-\dfrac{3e^{-t}}{-1}+t+k$$
When $t=0$, $x=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5&=2e^0+3e^0+0+k\\ 5&=5+k\\ k&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}+t\\ &=\dfrac{2}{e^{2t}}+\dfrac{3}{e^t}+t \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct velocity, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-4e^{-2t}-3e^{-t}+1\\ 0&=4e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}-1\\ &=4(e^{-t})^2+3e^{-t}-1 \end{aligned}$$
Let $m=e^{-t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4m^2+3m-1\\ &=(4m-1)(m+1)\\ m&=\dfrac{1}{4} \text{ or } m=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$e^{-t}=-1$ has no solution, since $e^{-t}>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-t}&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \ln e^{-t}&=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}\\ -t&=\ln 4^{-1}=-\ln 4\\ t&=\ln 4=1.386294361 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=\ln 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2e^{-2\ln 4}+3e^{-\ln 4}+\ln 4\\ &=2e^{\ln 4^{-2}}+3e^{\ln 4^{-1}}+\ln 4\\ &=2\times 4^{-2}+3\times 4^{-1}+\ln 4\\ &=\dfrac{2}{16}+\dfrac{3}{4}+\ln 4\\ &=\dfrac{7}{8}+\ln 4\\ &=2.261294361 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The particle is at rest when $t=\ln 4\approx 1.386$ seconds, at $x\approx 2.26$ m.
criteria: Forms the quadratic in $e^{-t}$, or equivalent merit

Arnold, a Year 12 student, runs his own business selling eco-friendly toothpaste. He supplies his product to a national supermarket chain.

The \textbf{price–demand function} $(p(x))$ models the relationship between the price per tube and the number of tubes demanded per week $(x)$. In general, price decreases as demand increases.

The \textbf{marginal price–demand function} $(p'(x))$, represents the rate of change of price with respect to quantity demanded, measured in tubes per week.

These functions are used in business to analyse the \textbf{price–elasticity of demand} and assist in determining profitable pricing strategies.

Arnold knows that when the demand is 50 tubes per week, the price is \$2.35 per tube.

He is also given the following marginal price–demand function $p'(x)=-0.015e^{-0.01x}$.

Find the \textbf{price–demand equation}, given the marginal price–demand function and the information above.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the marginal price–demand function:
$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=\int-0.015e^{-0.01x}\,dx\\ &=-0.015\int e^{-0.01x}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{-0.015}{-0.01}e^{-0.01x}+c\\ &=1.5e^{-0.01x}+c\end{aligned}$$
The price is $\$2.35$ per tube for $50$ tubes per week, so $p(50)=2.35$:
$$\begin{aligned}2.35&=1.5e^{-0.01(50)}+c\\ c&=2.35-0.91\\ &=1.44\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore p(x)=1.5e^{-0.01x}+1.44$$
criteria: Finds the correct integral with $+c$ and substitutes $x=50$ and $p=2.35$ correctly, or equivalent merit

The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{641_q30_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function

$$v_P=3t^2-6t+4,$$

parts.latex: Show that the equation for the velocity, $v_Q$, of car $Q$ is given by $v_Q=6t+4$.

Find the earliest time when car $P$ will pass car $Q$ after the race starts.

solutions.latex:
Car $Q$ has constant acceleration, so its velocity is linear in $t$: $v_Q=mt+c$.

At $t=0$: $v_Q=v_P=4$

At $t=4$:
$$v_Q=v_P=3(4)^2-6(4)+4=28$$
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{28-4}{4-0}=6\\ c&=4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v_Q=6t+4$$
criteria: Finds an equation in the form $y=mx+c$ with correct gradient and incorrect $y$-intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The signed area between curves $P$ and $Q$ represents the relative displacement between the cars.

The cars are at the same displacement from the start when the displacement between them is zero, so solve for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a\big(3t^2-6t+4-(6t+4)\big)\,dt&=0\\ \int_0^a\left(3t^2-12t\right)dt&=0\\ \Big[t^3-6t^2\Big]_0^a&=0\\ a^3-6a^2&=0\\ a^2(a-6)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=6$: the cars are the same distance from the start at $t=6$.

The integrand $3t^2-12t$ is the velocity of $P$ relative to $Q$, and $v_P>v_Q$ for $t>4$.

Hence car $P$ passes car $Q$ 6 seconds after the start of the race.

1032.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line such that its velocity in metres per second, $v$, is given by the equation below, where $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

$$v=2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}$$

parts.latex: What is the particle's initial speed?

can_use: Discriminant and the nature of roots

parts.latex:
What is the particle's change in displacement in the first 4 seconds?

Leave your answer in exact form.
Determine the particle's exact acceleration at $t=5$.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=2+0\\&=2\text{ ms}^{-1}\end{aligned}$$

$t>0$ and $t^2+1>0$, since square values must be positive.

$\therefore\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge0$, since the quotient of two positives is positive.

$\therefore 2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge2$

$\therefore v$ is always positive and never equals zero, so the particle is never at rest.

Or, using the discriminant: if the particle is at rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}&=0\\2t^2+2+t&=0\\2t^2+t+2&=0\\\Delta&=1^2-4(2)(2)\\&=-15<0\end{aligned}$$
$\Delta<0$, so there is no solution: the particle is never at rest.
criteria: Shows $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge0$ with a partial justification, or reaches $2t^2+t+2=0$, or equivalent merit

For $0\le t\le1$, $x=5t$:
$$\begin{aligned}x(0)&=5(0)\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

For $t>1$:
$$x'(t)=3t^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\dfrac{1}{t^2}$$
Both terms are positive, so $x'(t)>0$ and $x(t)$ is increasing for $t>1$.

$\therefore$ the displacement is increasing for $t>0$.

$\therefore$ the particle never comes to rest.

Alternatively, as $t\to\infty$, $x'(t)\to0^+$ (an asymptote), so $x'(t)$ is never $0$.

parts.latex:
A particle is moving on a straight line with acceleration given by

$$\ddot{x}=12e^{-2t}+e^{-t}$$

where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds.

Initially the particle's velocity is $-6$ m/s and its displacement is 8 m.

Show that the displacement of the particle is given by

$$x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4.$$
Show that the particle comes to rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.

Find the displacement when the particle comes to rest.

Give a simplified, exact answer.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int\ddot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{12e^{-2t}}{-2}+\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+C\\&=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $\dot{x}=-6$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6&=-6-1+C\\C&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1$$
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int\dot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-6e^{-2t}}{-2}-\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+t+C_2\\&=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+C_2\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $x=8$:
$$\begin{aligned}8&=3+1+0+C_2\\C_2&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1=0$$
Multiplying by $e^{2t}$ gives a quadratic in $e^t$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6-e^t+e^{2t}&=0\\(e^t)^2-e^t-6&=0\\(e^t+2)(e^t-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $e^t=-2$ or $e^t=3$.

$e^t>0$, so $e^t=-2$ has no solution.
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=3\\t&=\ln3\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.

meta.marker_note: Full marks need $t=\ln3$ with $e^t=-2$ rejected.

1267.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=2e^t+4e^{-t}$, $t$ is in seconds and $v$ m/s. Initially, the particle is at the origin $O$.

parts.latex: What is its initial velocity?
Is the particle ever at rest? Give reasons.
Find the displacement function, $x$, of the particle, at time $t$ seconds.
Find the time when the particle is at $x=4$.(Give your answer in exact form)

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v(0)&=2e^0+4e^0\\&=6\end{aligned}$$

Since $2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all values of $t$,
$$2e^t+4e^{-t}>0$$
for all values of $t$.

$\therefore$ The particle will never be at rest.

meta.top_criterion_original: must state both ($2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all $t$); if proving $v=0$ then must show $e^{2t}=-2$
meta.marker_note: Must state both ($2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all $t$); if proving $v=0$ has no solution, must show $e^{2t}=-2$.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int(2e^t+4e^{-t})\,dt\\&=2e^t-4e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2e^0-4e^0+C\\C&=-2+4\\\therefore C&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=2e^t-4e^{-t}+2$$

When $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}2e^t-4e^{-t}+2&=4\\2(e^t-2e^{-t}-1)&=0\\e^t-\dfrac{2}{e^t}-1&=0\\e^{2t}-e^t-2&=0 &&(\times e^t)\\(e^t-2)(e^t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^t+1>0$, $e^t-2=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=2\\t&=\ln2\end{aligned}$$

1272.stem: An object that was initially at the origin moves with velocity ($v$ m/s) given by $v=24+10t-t^2$.

parts.latex: Find the maximum speed of the object.
Find the acceleration when the object is at rest.
Find the total distance travelled by the object during the first 15 seconds.

solutions.latex:
$v=-t^2+10t+24$

The maximum speed is at the turning point of this concave down parabola, $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=-\dfrac{10}{2\times(-1)}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}v_{\max}&=24+10\times5-5^2\\&=49\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$

meta.concern: marking guideline answers maximum velocity (49 m/s at t = 5); speed |v| is unbounded for t > 12, so 'maximum speed' is only 49 m/s if the domain is limited (e.g. 0 <= t <= 12); guideline line '24 x 10 x 5 - 5^2' transcribed as printed (should be 24 + 10 x 5 - 5^2)
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $v_{\max}=24\times10\times5-5^2$ written as $24+10\times5-5^2$ (the value $49$ is unchanged).

solutions.latex:
The object is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-t^2+10t+24&=0\\t^2-10t-24&=0\\(t-12)(t+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $t\ge0$, $t=12$.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\&=-2t+10\\&=-2\times12+10\\&=-14\text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int(-t^2+10t+24)\,dt\\&=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin: $t=0$, $x=0$ gives $0=0+0+0+C$, so $C=0$.
$$x=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t$$
The object is at rest at $t=12$ (from (b)) and changes direction there, so find the displacement at $t=0$, $12$ and $15$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=0: & x&=0\\t&=12: & x&=-\dfrac{12^3}{3}+5\times12^2+24\times12=432\\t&=15: & x&=-\dfrac{15^3}{3}+5\times15^2+24\times15=360\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled}&=432+(432-360)\\&=504\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

1274.stem: The acceleration ($a$ m/s$^2$) of an object at time $t$ seconds is given by $a=\dfrac{-1}{(5t+1)^2}$. The object is initially 3 metres to the left of the origin travelling with velocity 1 m/s.

parts.latex: Find an expression for the object's velocity ($v$) at time $t$.
Find the limiting speed of the object.
Find the position of the object at the end of the 10$^{\text{th}}$ second. (Answer to the nearest metre)

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int a\,dt\\&=\int-(5t+1)^{-2}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-(5t+1)^{-2+1}}{(-2+1)\times5}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $v=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}1&=\dfrac{1}{5(5\times0+1)}+C\\C&=0.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$$

$v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$

As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}\to0$, so
$$v\to0.8$$
$\therefore$ The limiting speed of the object is $0.8$ m/s.

Integrating $v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int\left(\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8\right)dt\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{5}+0.8t+C\\&=\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{25}+0.8t+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3&=\dfrac{\ln(5\times0+1)}{25}+0.8\times0+C\\\therefore C&=-3\end{aligned}$$
$$x=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5t+1)+0.8t-3$$
When $t=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5\times10+1)+0.8\times10-3\\&=5.157\ldots\\&\approx5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The object is about $5$ m to the right of the origin.

1300.stem:
A particle $P$ is moving on the $x$ axis and its velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$, $t$ seconds after a given instant, is given by $v=t^2(3-t)$, $t\ge 0$.

When $t=2$, $P$ is observed to be $4\text{ m}$ from the origin $O$, in the positive direction of the $x-$axis.

parts.latex: Find the acceleration of $P$ when $t=2$.
The particle is initially at rest and is also at rest when $t=T$. Determine the distance of $P$ from $O$ when $t=T$.

solutions.latex:
Expanding, $v=3t^2-t^3$. Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$:
$$a=6t-3t^2$$
When $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=6(2)-3(2)^2\\&=12-12\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}t^2(3-t)&=0\\t&=0\text{ or }3\end{aligned}$$
So $T=3$.

Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int 3t^2-t^3\,dt\\&=t^3-\dfrac{1}{4}t^4+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=2$, $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=2^3-\dfrac{1}{4}\times 2^4+C\\C&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=t^3-\dfrac{1}{4}t^4$$
When $t=T=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=3^3-\dfrac{1}{4}\times 3^4\\&=6.75\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates and finds the constant to find the displacement equation, or equivalent merit

1328.stem:
A farm has a watering system which repeatedly fills a storage tank then empties its’ contents to water different sections of the farm. The volume of water $V$ (in cubic metres) in the tank at a time $t$ is given by the equation

$$V=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos t-2\sin t$$

where $t$ is measured in minutes.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$.
Determine whether the tank is initially filling or emptying, showing all calculations.
At what time does the tank first become completely full and what is its capacity when it is full?

Related and complementary angles.reason: Evaluating trig ratios of 7π/6 via related angle, beyond solving the equation.

Solving optimisation problems.reason: Differentiates a contextual function to find its maximum value.

solutions.latex: $$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2\sqrt{3}\sin t-2\cos t$$

The tank is emptying when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}<0$.

When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dt}&=2\sqrt{3}\sin(0)-2\cos(0)\\ &=2\sqrt{3}(0)-2(1)\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ tank is emptying at this time

The tank is full or empty when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\sin t-2\cos t&=0\\ 2\sqrt{3}\sin t&=2\cos t\\ \dfrac{\sin t}{\cos t}&=\dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{3}}\\ \tan t&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \ldots\end{aligned}$$
As the tank is initially emptying, the first value is when it is empty and the second is when it is full.

Tank first full when $t=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ minutes.
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)-2\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\\ &=6\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$

1565.stem:
The number of daylight hours on the $t^{th}$ day of the year in Sydney can be modelled by the following equation.

$$L(t)=12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]$$

parts.latex: Given that there were 14 hours of daylight 10 days before the start of the year, show that $k=2$.
How many days into the year will the number of daylight hours be increasing the fastest? (Answer to the nearest day)
Hence, find the number of daylight hours from that day until the end of the year.

solutions.latex:
When $t=-10$, $L=14$:

$$\begin{aligned} 14 &= 12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(-10+10)\right] \\ &= 12+k \\ k &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: substitutes in both values, then shows that $k=2$

solutions.latex:
The daylight hours increase fastest where $L'(t)$ is a maximum, so solve $L''(t)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} L'(t) &= -\dfrac{4\pi}{365}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \\ L''(t) &= -\dfrac{8\pi^2}{365^2}\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] &= 0 \\ \dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10) &= \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \\ t+10 &= 91.25,\ 273.75 \\ t &= 81.25,\ 263.75 \end{aligned}$$

Test which gives the maximum rate:

$$\begin{aligned} L'(81.25) &\approx -0.03 \\ L'(263.75) &\approx 0.03 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{daylight hours increase fastest } 264 \text{ days into the year}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the first or second derivative, or equivalent merit
Uses a correct method to find the steepest gradient, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct method used to find steepest gradient
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the handwritten $L''(t)$ had denominator $365$; it should be $365^2$ (answer unchanged).

solutions.latex:
Daylight hours from day $264$ to the end of the year ($t=365$):

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{264}^{365}\left(12+2\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right)dt &= \left[12t+\dfrac{365}{\pi}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right]_{264}^{365} \\ &= 4399.90137-3051.81796 \\ &= 1348\text{ hours (nearest hour)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct bounds of integral chosen, or equivalent merit

1627.stem: The velocity of a particle travelling on the $x$ axis is given by $v(t)=\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $t\ge 0$.

parts.latex: Show that the particle is stationary when $t=1$.
Explain why the particle is moving to the left for all times $t>1$.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds, correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}v(1)&=\dfrac{1}{1+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
So the particle is stationary at $t=1$.

meta.top_criterion_original: must show substitution AND concluding statement
meta.marker_note: Must show the substitution and a concluding statement.

solutions.latex:
$$a(t)=v'(t)=-\dfrac{1}{(t+1)^2}$$
$a(t)<0$ for all $t\ge0$, so $v$ is decreasing.

Since $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, $v<0$ for all $t>1$, so the particle always moves to the left for $t>1$.
criteria: Mathematical reasoning, e.g. finding $a(t)$ or use of inequalities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$v(0)=\dfrac{1}{2}>0$, $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, so the direction changes at $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right}\\v&<0 &&\text{for } t>1 &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
So the distance is
$$d=\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt+\left|\int_1^3\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_0^1+\left|\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_1^3\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}-(0-0)+\left|\ln4-\dfrac{3}{2}-\ln2+\dfrac{1}{2}\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}+\ln2-\ln4+1\\&=\ln\dfrac{2\times2}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The distance travelled is $0.5$ m.

1636.stem: A toxic substance in a lake is degrading naturally according to the formula $A(t)=3000m^{-0.2t}$, where $A$ is the number of grams of the substance remaining at $t$ years and $m>0$ is a constant.

parts.latex: If $A=2400$ after 6 years, find the value of $m$ correct to 1 decimal place.
Fish can be reintroduced to the lake once the rate of change of the toxic substance is greater than $-20$. After how many years can fish be reintroduced? Answer to one decimal place.
People can swim in the lake once the amount of the toxic substance is less than 50. In how many years can this happen, to the nearest year?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=6$ and $A=2400$:
$$\begin{aligned}2400&=3000m^{-0.2(6)}\\\dfrac{4}{5}&=m^{-\frac{6}{5}}\\m&=\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{-\frac{5}{6}}\\&=1.2\text{ (1 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Some students gave $0.8$.

solutions.latex:
With $m=1.2$, $A(t)=3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}$. Fish can be reintroduced when $A'(t)>-20$:
$$\begin{aligned}3000\ln(1.2)\times(-0.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\-600\ln(1.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<\dfrac{1}{30\ln1.2}\end{aligned}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}-0.2t\ln1.2&<-\ln(30\ln1.2)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln(30\ln1.2)}{0.2\ln1.2}\\&=46.5993724\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Fish can be reintroduced after $46.6$ years (1 d.p.).
criteria: Correct change of base or similar operation, or equivalent merit
Writes $A'(t)>-20$ with the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The amount is less than 50 when
$$\begin{aligned}3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<50\\-0.2t\ln1.2&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{60}\right)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)}{-0.2\ln1.2}\\&=112.283611\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ It is safe to swim after 113 years.

Determine the population of bacteria after 12 hours.
Find the time it takes for the population to reach 100,000 bacteria. Leave your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
The population triples every $4$ hours, so $P(4)=3\times100=300$:
$$\begin{aligned} 300&=100e^{4k} \\ 3&=e^{4k} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k=\dfrac{\ln 3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(12)&=100e^{12\times\frac{\ln 3}{4}} \\ &=100\times e^{\ln 3^3} \\ &=2700 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

Setting $P(t)=100\,000$ and using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 100\,000&=100e^{\frac{t\ln 3}{4}} \\ 1000&=e^{\ln 3^{\frac{t}{4}}} \\ 1000&=3^{\frac{t}{4}} \\ \dfrac{t}{4}&=\log_3 1000 \\ t&=\dfrac{4\ln 1000}{\ln 3} \\ &\approx25.15 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
Converting the decimal part to minutes:
$$\begin{aligned} t&\approx25+0.15\times60 \\ &=25 \text{ hours } 9 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

1707.stem:
A particle is moving such that its displacement in metres after $t$ seconds is given by the equation

$$x=-1.5+3\sin 2t$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of x = -1.5 + 3 sin 2t for 0 <= t <= 2 pi, range -4.5 to 1.5, crossing zero four times

parts.latex: State the maximum displacement of the particle.
can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.latex: Find the first four times when the particle is at the origin.

solutions.latex:
The maximum value of $\sin(2t)$ is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x_{\max}&=-1.5+3\times1 \\ &=1.5 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{373_q21_s1}

The particle is at the origin when $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1.5+3\sin(2t)&=0 \\ 3\sin(2t)&=1.5 \\ \sin(2t)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$; sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, and the pattern repeats every $2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 3\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

1708.stem:
A particle travels in a straight line. Its velocity $\dot{x}$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\dot{x}=\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)\ \text{metres per second}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: velocity-time graph: parabola through (0, 9), (1, 0), (3, 0) with minimum (2, -3)

parts.latex: Find the expression for the particle's displacement $x$ in terms of $t$, if the particle was initially at $x=2$.
Find an expression for the particle's acceleration in terms of $t$.
At what times is the particle at rest?
Draw a velocity-time graph that represents the motion of this particle, showing all important features.
Find the total distance travelled between $t=0$ to $t=3$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int\dot{x}\,dt \\ &=\int\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt \\ &=t^3-6t^2+9t+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially ($t=0$) $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=0^3-6(0)^2+9(0)+C \\ C&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=t^3-6t^2+9t+2 \text{ metres}$$
criteria: Correct primitive with constant, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=\dfrac{d}{dt}(\dot{x}) \\ &=6t-12 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2-12t+9&=0 \\ t^2-4t+3&=0 \\ (t-3)(t-1)&=0 \\ t&=1 \text{ or } 3 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

meta.checked_source_ok: source's x is a slip for t; t=1,3 verified, notation only

criteria: Shows the intercepts correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The distance is the area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, so split where the velocity changes sign ($t=1$, part (c)):
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x}&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving in the positive direction} \\ \dot{x}&<0 &&\text{for } 1<t\le3 &&\text{moving in the negative direction} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=\int_0^1\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt+\left|\int_1^3\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt\right| \\ &=\Big[t^3-6t^2+9t\Big]_0^1+\left|\Big[t^3-6t^2+9t\Big]_1^3\right| \\ &=(1-6+9)-(0)+\Big|(27-54+27)-(1-6+9)\Big| \\ &=4+|-4| \\ &=8 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct evaluation of both integrals, or equivalent merit
Correct integral expression split at $t=1$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The level of a local dam is being monitored. After $t$ days, the rate at which the volume of water in the dam is changing is given by

$$R=\dfrac{1\,000}{1+t}-500$$

where $R$ is the rate of change of the volume of water in the dam, measured in megalitres per day.

The volume of water in the dam at the end of the fifth day of monitoring was half the volume at the end of the fourth day.

Find an expression for the volume of water $V$ in the dam, $t$ days after the monitoring began.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\int R\,dt \\ &=\int\left(\dfrac{1000}{1+t}-500\right)dt \\ &=1000\ln|1+t|-500t+C \end{aligned}$$
The volume at the end of day $5$ is half that at the end of day $4$, so $V(4)=2V(5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000\ln5-2000+C&=2\left(1000\ln6-2500+C\right) \\ 1000\ln5-2000+C&=2000\ln6-5000+2C \\ C&=1000\ln5-2000-2000\ln6+5000 \\ &=1000\left(\ln5-2\ln6\right)+3000 \\ &=1000\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3000 \\ &=1000\left(\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore V=1000\ln|1+t|-500t+1000\left(\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3\right)$$

parts.latex: A particle, initially at the origin, moves in a straight line with velocity $v=8-4t$ metres per second. What is the total distance the particle travels in the first 4 seconds?

solutions.latex:
The velocity is zero when $8-4t=0$, so the particle turns at $t=2$.

Integrating with $x(0)=0$ gives $x=8t-2t^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(2) &= 16-8=8 \\ x(4) &= 32-32=0 \end{aligned}$$
The particle goes out $8$ m and back $8$ m, so the total distance is
$$8+8=16 \text{ m}$$

parts.latex:
The number $N$ of flies at the Longueville rubbish dump after $t$ weeks is given by the formula $N=N_0e^{0.04\,t}$, where $N_0$ is the initial number of flies.

Which expression represents the number of weeks it takes until the rubbish dump has doubled its population of flies?

This is option D.

1738.stem:
A tank contains 200 litres of petrol. More petrol is pumped into the tank for 20 minutes, until it is full.

The volume flow rate $R$ of petrol, in litres per minute, is given by

$$R=4\,(20-t)$$

parts.latex: Find a formula for the volume $V$ of petrol in the tank after $t$ minutes, where $t\le 20$.
How many litres of petrol were in the tank when it was full?
How long did it take to half fill the tank? (answer in minutes)

solutions.latex:
The flow rate is the rate of change of volume.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=R=4(20-t)=80-4t$$
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \int(80-4t)\,dt \\ &= 80t-2t^2+C \end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $V=200$, so $C=200$.
$$\therefore\ V=80t-2t^2+200$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The tank is full when the flow stops, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4(20-t) &= 0 \\ t &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} V(20) &= 80(20)-2(20)^2+200 \\ &= 1000 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

Half of the full volume of $1000$ L is $500$ L.
$$\begin{aligned} 80t-2t^2+200 &= 500 \\ 2t^2-80t+300 &= 0 \\ t^2-40t+150 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1600-600}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1000}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$t=35.811$ or $t=4.1886$.

The tank is full at $t=20$, so $t=35.811$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ t=4.1886 \text{ minutes (4 min 11 s)}$$
criteria: Forms the correct quadratic and solves it, or equivalent merit

1770.stem: The motion of a particle is given by $x=10t+4e^{-3.5t}-4$, where $x$ is the displacement from the starting position in metres and $t$ is time after the initial position in seconds.

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.
Sketch the velocity-time graph.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-3.5t}\right)=-3.5e^{-3.5t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10+4\times(-3.5)e^{-3.5t} \\ &= 10-14e^{-3.5t} \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10-14e^0 \\ &= -4\text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), the velocity is $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=10-14e^{-3.5t}$.

As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-3.5t}\to 0$, so $v\to 10$: the graph has the horizontal asymptote $v=10$.

The $t$-intercept is where $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10-14e^{-3.5t} &= 0 \\ e^{-3.5t} &= \dfrac{5}{7} \\ -3.5t &= \ln\dfrac{5}{7} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{5}{7}}{-3.5} \\ &= -\dfrac{2\ln\frac{5}{7}}{7} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{382_q23_s1}

1822.stem:
Light intensity is measured in lux. The light intensity, $I$ lux, a distance $d$ metres below the surface of the lake is given by:

$$I=6000e^{-kd}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex:
The light intensity 6 metres below the surface of the lake is 1000 lux.

Find the value of $k$, correct to four decimal places.
At what rate, in lux per metre, is the light density decreasing 6 metres below the surface of the lake, correct to the nearest lux?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $d=6$ and $I=1000$ into $I=6000e^{-kd}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000 &= 6000e^{-6k} \\ \dfrac{1}{6} &= e^{-6k} \\ \dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{6}}{-6} &= k \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=0.29862\ldots=0.2986\text{ (4 d.p.)}$$

The rate of change of the intensity is $\dfrac{dI}{dd}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dd} &= -0.2986\times 6000e^{-0.2986d} \\ &= -0.2986I \end{aligned}$$
When $d=6$, $I=1000$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dd} &= -0.2986\times 1000 \\ &= -298.6 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $-0.2986\times 6000\times e^{-0.2986\times 6}=-298.6$.

So the intensity is decreasing at about $299$ lux per metre.

parts.latex:
The motion of a particle moving in a horizontal line is given by $x=5t\,e^{-3t}$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle in cm and $t$ is the time in minutes.

Determine the time when the particle is at rest.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when the velocity is zero. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=5t & v&=e^{-3t}\\ u'&=5 & v'&=-3e^{-3t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 5e^{-3t}+5t\left(-3e^{-3t}\right) \\ &= 5e^{-3t}-15te^{-3t} \\ &= 5e^{-3t}(1-3t) \end{aligned}$$
$v=0$ needs $5e^{-3t}(1-3t)=0$. Since $5e^{-3t}\ne 0$ for all $t$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-3t &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest after $\dfrac{1}{3}$ minute (or $20$ seconds).

1857.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line and its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by:

$$v=2-\dfrac{4}{t+1}$$

parts.latex: Determine the initial velocity.
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=1$.
Find an expression for the acceleration of the particle at time $t$.
Explain why the force is always to the right for all $t\ge 0$.
Describe the motion of the particle as $t\to\infty$.

The initial velocity is at $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v(0)&=2-\dfrac{4}{0+1} \\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{initial velocity }2\text{ m/s to the left}$$

The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2-\dfrac{4}{t+1} \\ \dfrac{4}{t+1}&=2 \\ t+1&=2 \\ t&=1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest when $t=1$.

Acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Write $v=2-4(t+1)^{-1}$:

1912.stem:
An object moves along the number line so that its displacement ($x$ metres) from the origin is given by:

$$x(t)=12-2t+12\log_e(t+3)$$

where time $t$ is measured in seconds.

parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=3$.
In which direction is the particle moving when $t>3$ ? Justify your statement with mathematical working or in words.
can_use: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Initially means $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 12-0+12\ln 3 \\ &= 12+12\ln 3 \\ &\approx 25.2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is } 12+12\ln 3\approx 25.2\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$

The particle is at rest when the velocity $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}$$
When $t=3$:
$$v=-2+\dfrac{12}{6}=0$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest when $t=3$.

For $t>3$ we have $t+3>6$, so
$$\dfrac{12}{t+3}<\dfrac{12}{6}=2 \quad\text{and hence}\quad v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}<0$$
$\therefore$ the velocity is negative, so the particle moves in the negative direction (to the left).
criteria: Shows $v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}$ and attempts to find its sign, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A substance decomposes at a rate that is proportional to the mass of the substance remaining. The remaining mass (M) can be modelled using the formula $M=M_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is the time in hours, $M_0$ is the initial mass and $k$ is a constant.

Initially there is 30 kg of the substance. After 24 hours half of the substance has decomposed.

Determine how long it will take for 90% of the substance to decompose.

solutions.latex:
Half decomposes after $24$ hours, so $M=15$ when $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} 15 &= 30e^{-24k} \\ e^{-24k} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln2}{24} \end{aligned}$$
$90\%$ decomposed leaves $10\%$, so $M=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 30e^{-kt} \\ e^{-kt} &= \dfrac{1}{10} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln10}{k} \\ &= \dfrac{24\ln10}{\ln2} \\ &\approx79.7 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $e^{-kt}=\dfrac{1}{10}$ with the correct $k$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $M=15$ and $t=24$ into the formula, or equivalent merit

1960.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. It’s displacement, $x$ metres, from the origin, $O$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t\ge0$, is given by $x=4+3te^{-2t}$

parts.latex: Show the velocity of the particle is given by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3e^{-2t}\left(1-2t\right)$.
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Find the greatest possible total distance the particle could travel.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of the constant $4$ is $0$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(3te^{-2t}\right)$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3t & v&=e^{-2t}\\ u'&=3 & v'&=-2e^{-2t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=3e^{-2t}+3t\cdot\left(-2e^{-2t}\right)\\ &=3e^{-2t}-6te^{-2t}\\ &=3e^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to differentiate using the product rule

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$. At $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=3e^{-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}\left(1-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=3e^{-1}(1-1)\\ &=0\end{aligned}$$
Hence the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The particle starts at $x=4$. Since $3e^{-2t}\ne0$, $v=0$ only when $1-2t=0$, that is at $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving right}\\ v&<0 &&\text{for }t>\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
At the turning point:
$$x=4+3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-1}=4+\dfrac{3}{2e}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $x=4+\dfrac{3t}{e^{2t}}\to4+0=4$, approached from above but never reached.

Distance travelled moving right: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.

Distance travelled moving left, back towards $x=4$: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{greatest total distance}=\dfrac{3}{2e}+\dfrac{3}{2e}=\dfrac{3}{e}\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Calculates distance travelled in first half of journey, namely $\dfrac{3}{2e}$ metres

1986.stem:
A particle with velocity, $v\,ms^{-1}$ moves along a straight line from a fixed point $O$

$$v=-4\cos t$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

It is initially 1 metre to the right of the origin.

parts.latex: When, and where, does the particle first come to rest?

Show that the total distance travelled by the particle between $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is

$(8-2\sqrt{3})$ metres.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$; the first time after $t=0$ is the smallest positive solution:
$$\begin{aligned}-4\cos t&=0\\ \cos t&=0\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$
For the position, integrate the velocity and use $x=1$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int-4\cos t\,dt\\ &=-4\sin t+C\\ 1&=0+C\\ x&=-4\sin t+1\end{aligned}$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x=-4+1=-3$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first comes to rest at }t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s, at }x=-3\text{ (3 m to the left of the origin)}$$
criteria: Finds $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and an expression for $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$v=-4\cos t$ changes sign at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so find the distance in each part separately:
$$\begin{aligned}v&<0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&\text{moving left}\\ v&>0 &&\text{for }\dfrac{\pi}{2}<t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3} &&\text{moving right}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=-4\end{aligned}$$
The particle moves left, so the distance travelled in this part is $4$ m.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\\ &=-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right)\\ &=4-2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total distance}=4+\left(4-2\sqrt{3}\right)=\left(8-2\sqrt{3}\right)\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in one of the two intervals, or equivalent merit
Identifies that the direction changes at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, or equivalent merit

1992.stem:
A prototype rocket which is initially at rest, takes off from a launchpad on the ground. It has a time of flight of $T$ seconds, and $t$ is the time in seconds, where $0\le t\le T$.

The velocity of the rocket, $v\,ms^{-1}$, is given by:

$$v(t)=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$

parts.latex:
Shortly after the rocket takes off, the engine stops and it begins to descend towards the ground.

Find the time at which the rocket begins to descend.
Before the rocket starts to descend it reaches its maximum velocity. Find the time it takes for the rocket to achieve its maximum velocity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The rocket rises while $v>0$ and begins to descend when $v$ returns to $0$ after take-off:
$$0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi,\ \ldots$$
$t=0$ is the take-off, and for $0<t<10$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)>0$ so $v>0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket begins to descend at }t=10\text{ s}$$
criteria: Sets $v=0$ and finds $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For maximum velocity, $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=0$. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=0.5e^t & v&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ u'&=0.5e^t & v'&=\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dv}{dt}&=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+0.5e^t\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ &=0.5e^t\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\right)\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=0\\ \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}\end{aligned}$$
The rocket is rising for $0<t<10$, so $0<\dfrac{\pi t}{10}<\pi$. Tangent is negative in the second quadrant, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=\pi-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)\approx2.837$$
$$t\approx2.837\cdot\dfrac{10}{\pi}\approx9.03\text{ s}$$
$v=0$ at $t=0$ and at $t=10$ and $v>0$ between them, so this stationary point is the maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket reaches its maximum velocity after }9.03\text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Differentiates and forms $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}$, or equivalent merit

The population of parrots, $P$, is modelled by the function $P=P_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is time in years since May 2004.

parts.latex: Show that $P_0=2500$.
Find the value of $k$. (Answer correct to four decimal places).
If the population continues to decrease in this manner, what will be the expected population in May 2024? Answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$ the population is $P=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}2500&=P_0e^{-k\cdot 0}\\&=P_0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P_0=2500$$

In May 2014, $t=10$ and $P=1750$, with $P_0=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}1750&=2500e^{-10k}\\\dfrac{7}{10}&=e^{-10k}\\\ln\dfrac{7}{10}&=-10k\\k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{7}{10}\\&=0.0357\ \text{(to 4 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$$

2292.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of v against t: downward parabola from v=4 at t=0, crossing the t-axis at t=2, with the area from 0 to 3 shaded

parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.
Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

solutions.latex:
The velocity $v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$ is a concave-down parabola, so its maximum is at the turning point, where $v'(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}v'(t)&=-4t+2\\0&=-4t+2\\t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ s}$$
criteria: Recognises the maximum occurs at the turning point, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for recognising the maximum occurs at the turning point; 1 for $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2t^2+2t+4&=0\\-2\left(t^2-t-2\right)&=0\\-2(t-2)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=2$ or $t=-1$; since $t\ge 0$, $t=2$.

Integrate the velocity to find the position.
$$x(t)=\int v\,dt=-\dfrac{2t^3}{3}+t^2+4t+C$$
Initially $x(0)=4$, so $C=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}x(2)&=-\dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}+2^2+4\times 2+4\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is }\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$
criteria: Integrates to find $x(t)$, or equivalent merit
Factorises and solves $v=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for factorising and solving $v=0$; 1 for integrating to get $x(t)$; 1 for $x(2)=\dfrac{32}{3}$ m
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: -16/3+4+8+4 = 32/3.

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$, at $t=2$ (part (b)), so the distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, counting the part below the axis as positive.

\exfigure{162_q15_s1}

$$\int_0^2 v\,dt+\left|\int_2^3 v\,dt\right|$$
Using the antiderivative $F(t)=-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3+t^2+4t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance}&=F(2)-F(0)+\big|F(3)-F(2)\big|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}-0+\left|3-\dfrac{20}{3}\right|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}+\dfrac{11}{3}\\&=\dfrac{31}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is }\dfrac{31}{3}\text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the two integrals, the second in absolute value, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particle is moving on the $x$ axis. Its velocity, $v$ metres per second, at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=3-6\cos t$.

Initially the particle is at 4 metres on the right of the origin.

Which expression is the displacement function in terms of $t$ ?

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\int(3-6\cos t)\,dt\\&=3t-6\sin t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially $x(0)=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=0-0+C\\C&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x(t)=3t-6\sin t+4$, which is option A.

parts.latex: The acceleration of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $a=4t+4$ . Initially the particle has a velocity of $-30$ m/s. When is the particle at rest?

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the integral of acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int(4t+4)\,dt\\&=2t^2+4t+c\end{aligned}$$
Initially $v=-30$, so when $t=0$, $c=-30$.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=2t^2+4t-30\\&=2(t^2+2t-15)\\&=2(t+5)(t-3)\end{aligned}$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$, so $t=-5$ or $t=3$. Since $t\ge 0$, $t=3$, option C.

2409.stem: The population of ants is growing exponentially according to the equation $P=50e^{kt}$ , where $t$ is the time in days after the insect is first counted. After four days, it is observed that the population has doubled from the initial amount.

parts.latex: Find the initial number of ants and show that $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$
At what rate (to the nearest whole number) is the population increasing at day 15?
How many days will it take for the number of ants to first reach 1500?

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $P_0=50e^0=50$, so the initial number of ants is $50$.

After four days the population has doubled, so $P=100$ when $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}100&=50e^{4k}\\e^{4k}&=2\\4k&=\ln 2\\k&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the initial number of ants, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $P=50e^{kt}$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=50k\,e^{kt}$$
At $t=15$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=50\times\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\times e^{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\times 15}\\&\approx 117\text{ ants per day}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us. Checked: 116.57.

solutions.latex:
Put $P=1500$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$ and take natural logs.
$$\begin{aligned}1500&=50e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\30&=e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t&=\ln 30\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 30}{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2}\\&\approx 19.6\\&\approx 20\text{ days}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms and simplifies $30=e^{kt}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particle is moving in a straight line such that its displacement $x$ metres at time $t$ seconds from the origin is given by the equation $x=k\cos(at+b)$, where $a$, $b$ and $k$ are constants.

The particle is stationary when $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ldots$.

The initial acceleration of the particle is $6\sqrt{3}\ \text{ms}^{-2}$.

What could be the values of $a$, $b$ and $k$?

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary at $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12}$. Every second stationary time is one period apart, so
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{17\pi}{12}-\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\pi \quad\text{so}\quad a=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$$
Test option D, $x=-3\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 6\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ \text{acceleration} &= 12\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$v=0$ when $2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\pi,\ 2\pi,\ 3\pi,\ldots$ (the first value of $2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ for $t\ge0$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$), giving $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ldots$ as required.

At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{acceleration} &= 12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 12\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= 6\sqrt{3}\ \text{ms}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
Options B and C also have $a=2$ and the same stationary times, but their initial acceleration is $-6\sqrt{3}$, so only D fits.

meta.format_note: Source wrote the stationary condition as 0, pi, 2pi... 'taking the positive values'; written here as pi, 2pi, 3pi (t>0). Rejection of A, B, C added by us and checked: B has initial acceleration 12cos(-5pi/6)=-6sqrt3, C has -12cos(pi/6)=-6sqrt3, A has a=4.

2440.stem:
Ben is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven ($^\circ$C) at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.

parts.latex: What was the initial temperature of the oven?
Calculate the average rate at which the temperature changes per minute from $t=25$ to $t=75$, correct to two decimal places.

Ben can place the pizza in the oven when the instantaneous rate of change of temperature is less than or equal to $1^\circ$C per minute.

Given that Ben turned the oven on at 10:30 am, find the earliest time that Ben can place the pizza in the oven, correct to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
At the start, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 175-150\times(0.9)^{0} \\ &= 175-150 \\ &= 25^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; the single 1-mark row was written by us.

solutions.latex:
The average rate of change is $\dfrac{T(75)-T(25)}{75-25}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T(25) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times25} \\ &\approx 86.4265 \\ T(75) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times75} \\ &\approx 144.11633 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Average rate} &= \dfrac{144.11633-86.4265}{75-25} \\ &\approx 1.15^\circ\text{C/minute} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $T(25)$ and $T(75)$ and sets up the average rate, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. Checked: 57.6898/50=1.1538.

solutions.latex:
The instantaneous rate of change is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Differentiating with $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=ka^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -150\times0.2\times(0.9)^{0.2t}\times\ln0.9 \\ &= -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} \end{aligned}$$
The cut-off is where $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} &= 1 \\ (0.9)^{0.2t} &\approx 0.316374 \\ 0.2t &\approx \log_{0.9}0.316374 \\ t &\approx \dfrac{5\ln0.316374}{\ln0.9} \\ &\approx 54.6\ \text{minutes} \end{aligned}$$
The rate $-30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t}$ decreases as $t$ increases, so it is $\le1$ for $t\ge54.6$. To the nearest minute this is $55$ minutes after $10{:}30$ am.
$$\text{Time}=10{:}30\ \text{am}+55\ \text{min}=11{:}25\ \text{am}$$

2449.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis so that its position, in metres, at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$x=2\ln(t^2+3)-t$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand diagram of the motion on a line: at rest at t=1 and t=3, particle path between

parts.latex: Determine the times when the particle is at rest.

Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first second.

Leave your answer in the form $\ln\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)-c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.
Find the maximum velocity of the particle.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of position, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln\left(t^2+3\right)=\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}$.
$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2\times\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}-1=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4t}{t^2+3} &= 1 \\ 4t &= t^2+3 \\ t^2-4t+3 &= 0 \\ (t-1)(t-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=1 \text{ or } t=3\ \text{seconds}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the velocity to see whether the particle changes direction in the first second.
$$v=\dfrac{4t-t^2-3}{t^2+3}=-\dfrac{(t-1)(t-3)}{t^2+3}$$
For $0\le t<1$ both $(t-1)$ and $(t-3)$ are negative, so $v<0$. The particle moves in one direction only (it is at rest at $t=1$), so the distance is $x(0)-x(1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 2\ln3 \\ x(1) &= 2\ln4-1=4\ln2-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 2\ln3-(4\ln2-1) \\ &= \ln3^2-\ln2^4+1 \\ &= \ln9-\ln16+1 \\ &= \ln\dfrac{9}{16}+1 \\ &\approx 0.42\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

The 'v < 0 on [0,1], no change of direction' step was missing in the handwriting and added by us (checked: v = -(t-1)(t-3)/(t^2+3)). The answer ln(9/16) + 1 fits the requested form ln(a/b) - c with a = 9, b = 16, c = -1. Checked: 0.4246.

solutions.latex:
The acceleration is the derivative of velocity, using the quotient rule on $v=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$.
$$a=\dfrac{4(t^2+3)-4t\times2t}{(t^2+3)^2}=\dfrac{12-4t^2}{(t^2+3)^2}$$
Maximum velocity occurs where $a=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12-4t^2 &= 0 \\ t^2 &= 3 \\ t &= \sqrt{3} \quad(t\ge0) \end{aligned}$$
Test: $a>0$ for $0\le t<\sqrt{3}$ and $a<0$ for $t>\sqrt{3}$, so $v$ increases then decreases and has a maximum at $t=\sqrt{3}$ (between the rest times $t=1$ and $t=3$).
$$\begin{aligned} v_{\max} &= \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3+3}-1 \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1 \\ &\approx 0.1547\ \text{m/s} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{515_q28_s1}
criteria: Finds $t=\sqrt{3}$ and justifies a maximum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A heater converts electrical power, measured in watts, into heat in such a way that the heat produced is given by the function $h(x)=\left(f(x)\right)^2$.

The heater is plugged into a faulty socket which outputs $x=g(t)$ watts at time $t$ seconds.

The power output at time $t=1$ is 3 watts and is increasing at a rate of 4 watts per second.

By considering $h'(x)$ and using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dt}f\left(g(t)\right)=f'\left(g(t)\right)\times g'(t)$, find the rate of change of the heat produced at time $t=1$, given that $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.

solutions.latex:
Given $h(x)=\left[f(x)\right]^2$, differentiate with the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dh}{dx}=2f(x)f'(x)$$
The power output is $x=g(t)$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=g'(t)$.

Given: $g(1)=3$ (so $x=3$ when $t=1$), $g'(1)=4$, $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.

By the chain rule, $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{dh}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(x)f'(x)\,g'(t) \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$, $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(3)f'(3)g'(1) \\ &= 2\times5\times2\times4 \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

The question's hint 'f'(x) = f'(g(t)) x g'(t)' is the derivative of f(g(t)), not f'(x); left as printed (question not changed).

2487.stem:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the mass present.

The rate of change is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, where $k$ is a positive constant and $M$ grams is the mass present at any time, $t$ years.

parts.latex: Show that $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution to this equation.
If $68$g remains after a period of $2$ years, find $k$ correct to two significant figures.

Find the mass of the substance that remains after $6$ years.

Give your answer to one decimal place.
At what rate is the substance decaying after $6$ years ?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $M = 75e^{-kt}$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -k\cdot 75e^{-kt}$$
But $75e^{-kt} = M$, so
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$$
Hence $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution.

Substitute $M=68$ and $t=2$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 68 &= 75e^{-2k} \\ \dfrac{68}{75} &= e^{-2k} \\ -2k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ &\approx 0.049 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.049$$

Substitute $t=6$ and $k \approx 0.049$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 75e^{-6k} \\ &\approx 55.9 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M \approx 55.9 \text{ g}$$

meta.format_note: 55.9 g follows from using the rounded $k=0.049$ from part (b).

solutions.latex:
The rate of decay is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, with $k \approx 0.049$ and $M \approx 55.9$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt} &= -kM \\ &\approx -2.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the substance is decaying at approximately } 2.7 \text{ g/year}$$

2489.stem: The velocity, $\dot{x}$, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $\dot{x} = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.
Find an expression for the displacement of the particle, $x$, in terms of $t$.
Find when the particle first comes to rest.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $7$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=0$ into the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\cdot 0\right) \\ &= \cos 0 \\ &= 1 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$, so $C = 0$.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x} = 0$.
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) = 0$$
The first positive solution of $\cos\theta=0$ is $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 3 \text{ seconds}$$

The particle is at rest at $t=3$ and then reverses, so find the distance in two stages.
$$\begin{aligned} x(3) &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle moving along the $x$ axis at time $t$ is given by:

$$x=t^3+\ln\left(2t^3+1\right)\ \text{ for } t\ge 0$$

How many times is the particle stationary?

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3t^2+\dfrac{6t^2}{2t^3+1}$$
The particle is stationary when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2(2t^3+1)+6t^2&=0 \\ 3t^2(2t^3+3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Then $t=0$ or $t=-\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{2}}$, and only $t=0$ is valid for $t\ge0$.

Hence there is one solution.

2519.stem:
A quantity $Q$ of the radioactive isotope Carbon-14 decays according the equation of natural decay $Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$ where $Q_0$ is the initial mass of Carbon-14, $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the time in years.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time it takes to reduce to half its original mass. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years.

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $k$.

A fossilised leaf contains $9\%$ of its original amount of Carbon-14.

How old is the fossilised leaf? Give your answer correct to the nearest year.

solutions.latex:
After one half-life, $Q=\dfrac{Q_0}{2}$ when $t=5730$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{Q_0}{2} &= Q_0e^{-5730k} \\ 0.5 &= e^{-5730k} \\ \ln0.5 &= -5730k \\ k &= -\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln2}{5730} \end{aligned}$$
No penalty for writing $k=0.0001$ to 4 d.p.

The leaf has $9\%$ of its original amount, so $Q=0.09Q_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.09Q_0 &= Q_0e^{-kt} \\ 0.09 &= e^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Using $k=-\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}$, this is
$$0.09=e^{\frac{\ln0.5}{5730}t}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln0.09 &= \dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}\,t \\ t &= \dfrac{5730\ln0.09}{\ln0.5} \\ &\approx 19\,906 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the leaf is about } 19\,906 \text{ years old}$$
No penalty for incorrect rounding.
criteria: Correct equation $0.09=e^{-kt}$ or similar, or equivalent merit

2549.stem:
Since the introduction of the internet, the number of emails sent has been modelled using the exponential equation

$$M = M_0 e^{kt}$$

where $M$ is the number of emails sent worldwide, in millions, and $t$ is the number of years after the year 1980.

Records show that $45\,000$ emails were sent in 1980 and 306 billion emails were sent in the year 2020.

parts.latex: Find the values of $M_0$ and $k$, correct to three decimal places.
How many emails, to the nearest million, are expected to be sent in the year 2025?
Find the rate at which the number of emails sent increased in the year 2000, correct to the nearest million per year.

criteria: Finds the value of $M_0$ or $k$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added final decimal line $k\approx0.393$ (computed: ln 6,800,000 ≈ 15.73, /40 ≈ 0.393), since question asks three decimal places; source stopped at exact form

solutions.latex:
In 2025, $t = 45$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 0.045e^{45 \times \frac{1}{40}\ln 6\,800\,000} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679.032 \text{ million} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679 \text{ million (to the nearest million)} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiating $M = M_0e^{kt}$ gives
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = kM_0e^{kt}$$
In 2000, $t = 20$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt} &= \dfrac{1}{40}\ln(6\,800\,000) \times 0.045e^{20 \times \frac{1}{40}\ln(6\,800\,000)} \\ &\approx 46.153 \text{ million per year} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore \text{rate} \approx 46 \text{ million/year (to the nearest million/year)}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative of $M$ with respect to time, or equivalent merit

2558.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$$

where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.
Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

solutions.latex:
Method 1: maximum velocity occurs when $a(t) = 0$.

Differentiating $v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$,
$$a(t) = -4t + 2$$
$$\begin{aligned} -4t + 2 &= 0 \\ t &= 0.5 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: since velocity is a quadratic function, the maximum is at the vertex.
$$t = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{2}{2(-2)} = 0.5 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Attempts to solve $a(t) = 0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t) = 0$.
$$v(t) = 0 \text{ gives } t = -1 \text{ or } t = 2$$
Since $t \ge 0$, it first comes to rest at $t = 2$.

Since $x(0) = 4$, the position at $t = 2$ is
$$\begin{aligned} x(2) &= 4 + \displaystyle\int_0^2 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 4 + \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_0^2 \\ &= 10\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The particle is $10\dfrac{2}{3}$ metres to the right of the origin.
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in the first two seconds, or equivalent merit
Finds the time the particle comes to rest, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = 2$, so the distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the displacements on $[0,2]$ and $[2,3]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled} &= \int_0^2 v(t)\,dt + \left|\int_2^3 v(t)\,dt\right| \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \int_2^3 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_2^3 \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(3)^3 + (3)^2 + 4(3)\right) - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(2)^3 + (2)^2 + 4(2)\right)\right] \\ &= 10\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled by the particle in the third second, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A population, $P$, which is initially 40 500, varies according to the formula $P = 40500\,b^{\frac{-t}{5}}$ where $b$ is a positive constant and $t$ is time in years, $t \ge 0$

The population is 1500 after 15 years.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of decrease is 25 people per year.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $P = 1500$, $t = 15$ to find $b$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1500 &= 40500\,b^{-\frac{15}{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{27} &= b^{-3} \\ 27 &= b^3 \\ b &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
We want $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -25$.

Using $y = a^x$, $y' = \ln a \cdot a^x$ on $P = 40500 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 40500 \times \dfrac{-1}{5}\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \\ &= -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $-25$.
$$\begin{aligned} -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= -25 \\ 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{324\ln 3} \\ -\dfrac{t}{5} &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ t &= \dfrac{-5\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ &= 26.737\ldots \\ &\approx 26.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 26.7 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $b$, sets $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-25$ and finds a correct derivative, or equivalent merit

2606.stem: The water level, measured in meters, at a dam has been changing at a rate of $R = t^3 - 11t^2 + 35t - 29$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ years.

parts.latex: When is the water level decreasing most rapidly?
What is the change in water level of the dam for the 6 years?

solutions.latex:
The water level decreases most rapidly where $R$ is least, so find the stationary points of $R$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= 3t^2-22t+35 \\ &= (3t-7)(t-5) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dR}{dt}=0$ gives $t=\dfrac{7}{3}$ or $t=5$.

Nature, using the second derivative $\dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=6t-22$:
$$\begin{aligned} t=\dfrac{7}{3}:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=-8<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ t=5:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=8>0 &&\text{minimum, } R=-4\end{aligned}$$
Check the endpoints of the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:\ & R=-29\\ t=6:\ & R=1\end{aligned}$$
The least value of $R$ is $-29$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreases most rapidly at } t=0$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points and their nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The change in level is the integral of the rate:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6\left(t^3-11t^2+35t-29\right)dt &= \left[\dfrac{t^4}{4}-\dfrac{11t^3}{3}+\dfrac{35t^2}{2}-29t\right]_0^6 \\ &= -12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreased by } 12 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral, or equivalent merit
